The two series share no sources, the one resting on the republic's own statistics and the other on ESSR yearbooks and post-war archives; no weights, one using the structure of 1938 and the other that of 1990; and no benchmark, one a bilateral price comparison with Sweden, the other a purchasing-power-parity study of the Soviet republics fifty-two years later. That the Soviet-period series, extrapolated backwards over half a century of war, collectivisation and forced industrialisation, arrives within 4 per cent of an independently measured level is the strongest evidence available that the net error of the extrapolation is small. It cannot exclude errors that happen to offset, such as an overstatement of growth from hidden inflation in trade turnover against an understatement from the index-number assumptions. But the two index-number biases discussed below, late base-year weights and fixed value-added weights, would both understate growth and so would both place the backcast 1937--40 level above the interwar series; the overlap therefore tests their combined size. A net understatement of growth of as little as 0.1 percentage point a year over 1940--90 would place the Soviet-period series 5 per cent above the interwar series in every overlap year, which is not observed. Nor can the agreement be the product of a low benchmark offsetting understated growth: the 1990 level is, if anything, 3 per cent above the independent 2011-based estimate (Table~\ref{tab:overlaps}, panel b), which would push the backcast levels up, not down. Broadberry and Burhop regarded time-series projections as consistent with direct benchmarks when they agree within 10 per cent, and judged a thirty-year projection that landed within 4 per cent a success;\footnote{\autocite[323--6]{broad2007}; \autocite[933]{broad2008}.} the Estonian overlap meets that standard over a longer span in each of four consecutive years. The second overlap is less tidy, and instructively so. In 1990 the Soviet-period series stands 3.0 per cent above the modern series and in 1991 less than 1 per cent below it; thereafter the gap widens to \ovd{1992} per cent in 1992 and \ovd{1995} per cent by 1995. The agreement in 1990--1 validates the 1990 benchmark, and in particular the conversion from roubles to dollars: Bolotin's figure rests on purchasing-power parities, not exchange rates, and the modern series derives from an entirely independent ICP round, that of 2011, carried backwards with the World Bank's constant-price growth rates, so that two routes that share no data arrive at the same level within 3 per cent. The divergence after 1991 arises because the Soviet-period series continues to value the collapse of Soviet-era output at 1990 weights and, in trade, relies on deflated turnover figures that understate inflation: it records what happened to the Soviet-era economy, not what replaced it. The modern series is therefore preferred from 1991, the year in which the two agree. It is anchored on the MPD's 2011 figure for Estonia, 21,997~\intltwenty{} or 13,800~\intlnineteen{}, and carried back to 1990 with the World Bank's constant-price growth of GDP per head rather than with the MPD's own growth, because the two sources' Estonian growth rates converge only in 2011: the MPD's path implies a rise of 28 per cent between 1990 and 2011 where the national accounts record 69 per cent, so that its 1990 level, 17,247~\intltwenty{}, stands 32 per cent above the World Bank-based 13,033. An index with a late base year assigns to each sector the relative prices of the end of the period, and since the sectors that grew fastest were, as a rule, those whose relative prices fell, late weights give less importance to fast-growing sectors and so understate growth; conversely, early weights overstate it. Feinstein and Thomas put the point generally: an index with an early base `will always show a greater increase in quantities than one constructed with a base year late in the period'.\footnote{\autocite[516]{feinsteinthomas2002}.} This is the effect that Gerschenkron showed for Soviet machinery, and it was large in the Stalin period: Bergson's GNP for 1928--37 grows by 175 per cent at 1928 prices and by 62 per cent at 1937 prices.\footnote{\autocite[453]{gerschenkron1957}; \autocite[517]{feinsteinthomas2002}.} Three considerations establish that it is far smaller for the series presented here. First, the effect is concentrated in the early phases of industrialisation, when relative prices change fastest; Jonas and Sardy showed that `most of the action which leads to the Gerschenkron effect takes place early'.\footnote{\autocite[85]{jonassardy1970}.} For the post-war Soviet economy the measured effect is modest. When the CIA moved its base year from 1970 to 1982 prices, its estimate of Soviet GNP growth over 1951--84 fell by about half a percentage point a year, from 5.6 to 5.2 per cent for the 1950s and from 3.2 to 2.4 per cent for the 1970s; an earlier comparison of 1960, 1970 and 1976 prices produced differences of a few tenths of a point, which the CIA judged `not large'.\footnote{\autocite[8]{cia1990}; \autocite[23--4]{cia1982a}; \autocite[156]{harrison1993}.} Half a point a year over forty years compounds to roughly a fifth of the level; this indicates the order of magnitude to be expected for the post-war decades rather than a bound, since the Estonian extrapolation also spans the forced industrialisation of the 1940s and 1950s, in which the effect is largest. Second, the bound must therefore come from the data, and the series can be tested. If 1990 weights understated Estonian growth over 1940--90, the Soviet-period series would arrive in 1937--40 systematically above the interwar series, which is weighted by the prices of 1938. It does not: the four differences are small and of both signs. The structural change within industry, where the Gerschenkron effect originates, is moreover handled at a finer level than the aggregate weights suggest, since the 101 product series are aggregated within eleven branches with 1986 weights before the branches are combined. Third, the procedure is that of every comparable reconstruction of Soviet output: the CIA used 1970 weights for 1950--80 and 1982 weights for 1950--90, and Maddison found `nothing untoward' in it; Kuboniwa's and Ponomarenko's reconstructions of Russian GDP for 1961--90 use, among their variants, the fixed structure of Russia's 1990 GDP.\footnote{\autocite[312]{Maddison1998b}; \autocite[57, 62]{ponomarenko2002}.} Fourth, the result can be set beside series built on other weights. A chain-linked alternative would require annual current-price value-added by sector, which exists for no Soviet republic, and a 1938-weighted alternative would require the sectors of 1990 to be valued at 1938 prices, when several of them did not exist. Nor has a benchmark at factor cost ever been constructed for a Soviet republic: the single-year study that Alton's project produced for Hungary runs to 254 pages, and a comparable exercise for a republic without price statistics of its own would be a monograph in itself.\footnote{\autocite{alton_hungary}.} \subsection{Fixed value-added weights} A related assumption is that the ratio of value-added to gross output within each sector remained at its benchmark-year level. The war had destroyed people rather than plant: with a fifth of the population gone, productive capacity stood underused, and the first years of recovery, in which the investment ratio was still below the Soviet mean even on official data, rested on putting labour, increasingly immigrant labour directed from Russia, back to work on existing capital, the mechanism that Vonyó and Markevich identify across post-war East-Central Europe.\footnote{\autocite[108]{years_of_dependence}; \autocite[290]{vonyoinmorys2021}; \autocite[126--8]{baltichistorykasekamp2017}.} Agriculture tells a different story. Livestock output, halved by the war, was still 38 per cent below its 1938 level in 1950, the year after collectivisation; crop output recovered sooner, but the agricultural sector as a whole stood at 60--65 per cent of its 1938 level in 1945--6, fluctuated between 77 and 93 per cent of it in 1947--57, and exceeded it only in \sregain{Primarysectortotal}. The index shows a shallower trough than Mertelsmann's archival estimate, which puts output after collectivisation at perhaps 40 per cent of the 1939 level, but the two agree that the sector did not recover for a decade, and that the collective and state farms produced little more than a third of output in the early 1950s, the rest coming from private plots, which still supplied 28 per cent in 1960.\footnote{\autocite[156--8]{olaf_stalin}; \autocite[79--109]{feest2014}; \autocite[257]{klesment2009}; \autocite[160]{hansen1994}.} Nothing comparable to the Soviet famine of 1932--3 occurred, probably because the Baltic collectivisation of 1949 did not coincide with a procurement crisis and because, as Harrison has argued for Soviet agriculture generally, the system had by then learned to extract the surplus without destroying the herds.\footnote{\autocite[192--208]{harrison1996}.} The cost of war and collectivisation together was a lost decade and a permanent shift of effort towards animal husbandry, in which Estonia came to lead the Union in output per head, while crop output never again exceeded the level it reached in \speak{Crops}.\footnote{\autocite[234]{years_of_dependence}.} Between 1950 and 1968 Estonia experienced what Gerschenkron would have recognised as a classic burst of state-led industrialisation. Total GDP grew by \tgr{1950}{1968} per cent a year and income per head by \gr{1950}{1968} per cent, faster than in Finland, the Nordic countries or the Western core, though not than the Western periphery, whose Iberian and Greek members were in the middle of their own industrialisation (Table~\ref{tab:growth}). The engine was investment directed from Moscow into three complexes. The first was the oil-shale basin of the north-east, which fed two of the largest thermal power stations in the Union and raised electricity output from 2 billion kilowatt-hours in 1960 to 12 billion in 1970, two-thirds of it consumed outside the republic. The second was cotton textiles, expanded in Estonia rather than in cotton-growing Uzbekistan because Estonia had the skilled labour and the mills; the third, machine-building and electronics for the Union market.\footnote{\autocite[239]{years_of_dependence}; \autocite[41--7]{ahderajasalu1992}; \autocite[248--58]{pihlamagi2013}.} The pace was already slackening: industrial output had grown by 15 per cent a year in 1948--55 and grew by 9 per cent a year in the decade that followed, and the sovnarkhoz reform of 1957--65, which briefly placed industrial management in Tallinn, was Khrushchev's response to that deceleration across the Union rather than its cause. Baltic historiography has judged the reform favourably, perhaps more for the autonomy it conferred than for its results; it saw official industrial output double in seven years (the physical index used here rises by 80 per cent over 1957--64), with 70 per cent of investment going to industry and the share of light industry in the total deliberately reduced, and it was superseded in 1965 by the Kosygin reform and the recentralisation of enterprises.\footnote{\autocite[248--52]{pihlamagi2013}; \autocite[67--70]{purre1965}; \autocite[189]{years_of_dependence}.} The labour came partly from a countryside that collectivisation had released and partly from immigration: Estonia's population grew by half between 1950 and 1989 while the Estonian share of it, close to 97 per cent at the end of the war, had fallen to three-quarters by the census of 1959 and to little more than 60 per cent by that of 1989.\footnote{\autocite[158--217]{case_estonia}.} The expansion was interrupted once. In 1962 the crop index fell by 19 per cent and the primary sector by 9 per cent; total GDP grew by 2 per cent and income per head by less than 1 per cent, against about 5 per cent a year in the surrounding years (Tables~\ref{tab:series} and~\ref{tab:appsec1}). The check was the Estonian instance of the agricultural crisis that overtook the whole Union in 1962--3. Recent Russian studies trace that crisis to the restrictions placed on private plots and private livestock from 1958, which moved animals into collective herds that had no fodder for them, to the exhaustion of the virgin-lands and maize campaigns, and finally to the drought of 1963 in Kazakhstan and Siberia, which cut the Union grain harvest from 83 million tons in 1962 to 63 million. The leadership raised state purchase prices for livestock by 35 per cent and the retail prices of meat by 30 and of butter by 25 per cent from 1 June 1962, suppressed the strike that followed at Novocherkassk, and in the autumn of 1963 rationed bread in many cities and bought grain abroad on a scale without precedent.\footnote{\autocite[17--19]{belkharoev2024}; \autocite[111--13]{andreenkov2021}.} Estonia's harvest failed a year before the Union's. Its grain deliveries to the all-Union fund fell from 30,000 tons in 1961 to 13,000 in 1962, collective farms were gathering fir needles for fodder in the winter of 1962--3, and the herd, 307,000 cows at the start of 1963, was far short of the 432,000 that the seven-year plan had set for 1965.\footnote{\autocite[34--5, 55]{purre1964}, a pamphlet compiled from the republican press.} Crops recovered in 1963, when Estonian grain deliveries to the all-Union fund rose to more than twice their 1961 level as the rest of the Union went short, but livestock output stood just below its 1938 level from 1961 to 1964, and the primary sector as a whole was back at its 1961 level only in 1963 and above it in 1964. Whether the Estonian failure of 1962 owed more to the season or to the sowing plans and fodder policy that Purre documented cannot be settled from the index. What the index shows is that the crisis cost Estonia a year of growth rather than, as in much of the Union, a winter of bread queues: industry grew by 7 per cent in 1962, little below its pace in the years around it, and the loss was confined to the farms. How did this growth compare with that of the Union into which Estonia had been absorbed? Table~\ref{tab:relative} gives the answer, and it is not the one that either Soviet or nationalist accounts have assumed. Estonia entered the Union in 1940 with income per head \pctussr{1940} per cent of the Soviet average; it stood at \pctussr{1968} per cent in 1968 and at \pctussr{1989} per cent in 1989. The gap neither closed nor widened appreciably over half a century: Estonia grew with the Union, somewhat faster in the 1950s and 1960s and somewhat slower thereafter, and remained one of its two or three richest republics throughout. The result matches Soviet-era estimates that placed Estonia at 137--145 per cent of the Union average in 1960--70 by net material product, and agrees in direction, if not in magnitude, with the CIA's finding that Estonian national income per head grew faster than the Union's in 1961--9, 6.3 against 5.5 per cent a year on NMP-based data that overstate growth.\footnote{\autocite[169, 174]{schroeder1973}; \autocite[64--71]{bs_livingstandards1976}; \autocite[8--10]{cia1972}; \autocite[35--8]{bs_livingstandards1988}.} Did Moscow buy the loyalty of its western borderlands with investment? Investment per head in Estonia was above the Union average in the 1960s, second only to Kazakhstan, but the republic's share of investment in its own national income was below the Union average. Van Selm and Dölle's reconstruction of inter-republican transfers finds Estonia's net balance close to zero from 1966 to 1978, becoming a net recipient of 4--6 per cent of national income only after 1979 and of 13 per cent in 1988.\footnote{\autocite[22--9]{cia1972}; \autocite[53]{adirim1988}; \autocite[136--40]{vanselmdolle1993}.} For the years after 1966 for which transfers can be measured, Estonia's high income was not the product of net transfers; and over the period as a whole it was inherited rather than created, since the republic was richer than the Union at annexation and remained so in roughly the same proportion. The deceleration after 1968 was general and, by the late 1970s, complete. Income per head grew by \gr{1968}{1989} per cent a year over 1968--89 and by \gr{1973}{1989} per cent after 1973, and the sectoral peaks cluster in a single decade: food processing in \speak{Food}, construction in \speak{Construction}, electricity and oil-shale output in 1979--80, heavy industry in \speak{Heavyindustries}.\footnote{Electricity peaked in 1979 and fell by 9 per cent to 1985; oil-shale mining levelled off after the arrival of natural gas (\autocite[239]{years_of_dependence}; \autocite{taagepera2018}).} The turning point coincided with the Prague Spring and the end of Moscow's tolerance of regional economic autonomy, and with the year in which the Union as a whole ceased to converge on Western levels, ahead of most other European communist economies.\footnote{\autocite[203, 227--8]{years_of_dependence}.} The sources point to three causes. The Union-wide investment slowdown imposed by the tenth and eleventh five-year plans fell on a republic whose growth had been investment-led and whose labour reserves were exhausted: further expansion required immigration or capital deepening, and the planners, whose investment effort shifted eastwards to Siberia in the 1970s, increasingly withheld both; on official data the investment ratio in Estonia fell below the Soviet average by the mid-1970s and stayed there.\footnote{\autocite[128--63]{hanson2003}; \autocite[164--76]{kolde1978}; \autocite[441]{dienes1972}; \autocite[2]{ciasovietrep1970}.} The oil-shale complex, built on a resource that was expensive to mine and polluting to burn, lost its rationale once Siberian gas reached the Baltic.\footnote{\autocite[188--9]{olaf_stalin}.} And the gains in reported output after 1975 were increasingly nominal: Finnish and Estonian economists who compared the two economies in 1992 concluded that the rapid growth of Estonian industry to 1975 reflected real investment, but that `the further growth of production can be explained mainly by the change in prices'.\footnote{\autocite[39--40]{ahderajasalu1992}.} The physical indices used here confirm that judgement: industrial output grew by \sgr{Industrytotal}{1968}{1989} per cent a year after 1968, and the branches that continued to grow, textiles and other light industry, did so slowly, while cotton cloth output was flat from 1970.\footnote{\autocite[41]{ahderajasalu1992}.} The textile index itself fell by 14 per cent between 1972 and 1975 and did not regain its 1972 level until 1985 (Table~\ref{tab:appsec1}), the one sharp break in a branch that otherwise grew throughout the Soviet period; the sources consulted offer no explanation, and the authors record it rather than interpret it. Three further irregularities in the indices deserve mention. Construction, which had grown by about 9 per cent a year since 1950, peaked in \speak{Construction} and stagnated for the rest of the Soviet period as the Union-wide investment squeeze took hold; crop output fell by a quarter in each of the poor harvests of 1978 and 1981 that affected the Union as a whole; and the housing index, which is derived from construction activity and population and had grown by between 2 and 3 per cent a year since the 1950s, stopped growing in 1986, when completions began to fall from 13,500 dwellings a year in 1985 to 5,200 in 1991; its slight decline thereafter reflects the construction of the proxy rather than a physical loss of stock.\footnote{\autocite[134--50]{hanson2003}; \autocite[60, 66]{ahderajasalu1992}; \autocite[216]{wb1993estonia}.} Read through the lens of growth theory, the Soviet episode is coherent. The catch-up of 1950--68 is what the models predict when a capital-poor economy with high social capability is made to invest, and mid-century mass-production methods were congruent with Estonia's literate and urbanised labour force; the stagnation that followed is equally what they predict when the institutional condition fails. Extensive growth exhausted its inputs, and the system could not replace them with the productivity growth that flexible production, foreign technology and competition were delivering across the Gulf: the share of services in Estonian GDP was 42 per cent in 1990, barely above its interwar level, against about 60 per cent in Finland.\footnote{Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks}; \autocite[11--12]{ahderajasalu1992}; \autocite{klimantas2026soviet}.} Estonia's income relative to the Western core, which had risen from \pctwc{1950} per cent in 1950 to \pctwc{1968} per cent in 1968, fell back to \pctwc{1989} per cent by 1989, almost exactly its level of 1913. Two decades of Soviet growth had been cancelled by two decades of Soviet stagnation; by 1989 Greece, the poorest capitalist economy in Western Europe, had overtaken Estonia, one of the richest parts of the socialist world after Slovenia (Table~\ref{tab:relative}). \subsection{Transition and recovery} The transition compressed into four years a fall in income per head of \eeTROUGHpct{} per cent, deeper than the Depression and comparable only to the two world wars. The sectoral indices to 1991 show the collapse beginning in Soviet-era industry and construction, which were already shrinking at \sgr{Industrytotal}{1989}{1991} and \sgr{Construction}{1989}{1991} per cent a year before the rouble was abandoned. After 1991 the modern series records the loss of eastern markets and cheap Soviet inputs, the currency board of 1992 and the stabilisation that followed.\footnote{\autocite[1--8]{wb1993estonia}; \autocite[164--6]{norkus_restorations}; \autocite[482--509]{shteinbuka1993}.} By comparison with the other Soviet republics the fall was contained, probably because Estonia had less heavy industry to lose, 41 per cent of industrial value-added in 1990 against 48 in Latvia and 55 in Lithuania, and reoriented trade towards Finland and Sweden faster than any other successor state.\footnote{\autocite[184--6]{bolotin1992}; \autocite[22]{transition_greenes}; \autocite[117]{baltistates_smith_estonia}; \autocite[443--4]{transition_progress}.} Recovery from 1995 at \gr{1995}{2022} per cent a year carried Estonia from \pctwc{1995} per cent of the Western core in 1995 to \pctwc{2022} per cent in 2022, close to the \pctwc{1968} per cent reached in 1968 at the height of Soviet growth. Whether the market-era catch-up will continue or stall in the middle-income trap that Staehr describes is a question for another paper; the long series shows that Estonia converged on Western Europe under capitalism twice, in the 1930s and after 1995, and under planning once, briefly, before diverging again.\footnote{.}

A FINNISH MIRACLE THAT NEVER WAS % ============================================================= \section{A Finnish miracle that never was} \label{sec:finland} The comparison with Finland has shaped the way Estonians and their historians think about the twentieth century. The two peoples speak related languages, were shaped by Lutheran schooling and Swedish law, emancipated their peasantries early and built co-operative agrarian economies after 1918; in the Soviet period Finland, visible on television from Tallinn, became `proof of what Estonia would have been if the country had not ended up under the Soviet occupation'.\footnote{\autocite[83]{lepppantti2013}.} The scholarly version of the argument has two steps. The first is that the two countries stood at the same level before 1940: Dellenbrant wrote that their levels of development were `close to equal around 1940', Soviet-era comparisons of real wages put Estonian workers ahead of Finnish ones as late as 1966, and the White Book's estimate of the losses of occupation rests on the assumption that Estonia would have followed the Finnish path.\footnote{\autocite[206]{dellenbrant1992}; \autocite[251, 257]{klesment2009}; \autocite[141--74]{kukk2005}.} The second is that the gap observed in 1991, when Estonian living standards were put at 40 per cent of Finland's, measures the cost of Soviet rule.\footnote{\autocite[206]{dellenbrant1992}.} Sceptics have questioned both steps. Kõll argued in 1994 that the belief in Baltic--Nordic parity before the war was `misleading'; an Estonian economist of the 1930s had already written that `Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and even Latvia are ahead of us regarding their wealth'; and Norkus, working from the benchmark estimates, concluded that the gap `cannot only be considered as the legacy of the Soviet occupation'.\footnote{\autocite[201]{koll1994gap}; \autocite[131]{klesment2005}; \autocite[18]{norkus2016}; \autocite[154]{norkus_restorations}.} The new series allows the two steps to be examined year by year. Table~\ref{tab:relative} gives Estonian income per head as a percentage of Finland's at the benchmark years, and Table~\ref{tab:growth} the growth rates between them. In 1913 the two countries were indeed close: Estonia stood at \pctfin{1913} per cent of the Finnish level. In 1919, after wars that had damaged both, Finland the more severely in 1918, it stood at \pctfin{1919} per cent. The parity did not survive the 1920s. Finland grew by \grx{Finland}{1919}{1929} per cent a year to 1929 and Estonia by \gr{1919}{1929} per cent, and by 1929 Estonia was at \pctfin{1929} per cent of the Finnish level; the 1930s, in which Estonia's growth of \gr{1929}{1938} per cent a year was close to Finland's \grx{Finland}{1929}{1938} per cent, left the ratio at \pctfin{1938} per cent in 1938. Clark's 90 per cent, which Valge adopted and which has anchored the literature since, is thus too high by a sixth; Bocharnikova's finding that the purchasing power of wages in Estonia was only 4 per cent below Finland's in 1938 refers to urban wages alone and says nothing about the nearly two-thirds of the Estonian labour force on the land.\footnote{\autocite[81--2]{bocharnikova2021}.} The difference in 1938 was not one of social capability. Table~\ref{tab:structure} shows Estonian literacy above Finnish, Estonian university enrolment per head well above Finnish, and the same share of the labour force in agriculture; Table~\ref{tab:trade} shows both economies open, though Finland more so. The difference is better explained by resources and markets. Finland's forests, sawmills and pulp mills gave it an export staple for which Western demand recovered quickly after 1920 and which carried a growing engineering sector with it; Estonia's butter and bacon faced Danish competition and British quotas, and its industry had lost the only large market it had ever served.\footnote{\autocite[184, 198--200]{finlandeh01}; \autocite[193--210]{koll1994gap}.} The second step of the argument fares no better, though for a different reason. Soviet rule did open a gap, but the timing is not what the argument supposes. Finland lost the Second World War and paid reparations; Estonia was fought over twice and collectivised. In 1950 the ratio stood at \pctfin{1950} per cent, higher than in 1938, and in 1968, after the two decades of Soviet industrialisation examined above, at \pctfin{1968} per cent, the highest level since 1919. Measured against Finland, the first half of Soviet rule was a period of convergence. The divergence that the literature attributes to occupation is a phenomenon of its second half: between 1968 and 1989 Finland grew by \grx{Finland}{1968}{1989} per cent a year, half as fast again as the Western core, and Estonia by \gr{1968}{1989} per cent, so that the ratio fell to \pctfin{1973} per cent in 1973 and \pctfin{1989} per cent in 1989. Those who lived through it dated the divergence correctly: Dellenbrant, drawing on Kukk's calculations, placed its beginning in the late 1960s.\footnote{\autocite[205]{dellenbrant1992}.} What the new series adds is the magnitude. Expressed in logarithms, the Estonian shortfall against Finland was 0.29 in 1938 and 0.63 in 1989; almost half of the gap at the end of Soviet rule had opened before it began, and the whole of the increase after 1938 occurred after 1968. Two conclusions follow. The first concerns the use of Finland as a yardstick. Finland is a revealing comparator for Estonia, because the two economies had similar endowments of human capital, though not of natural resources or markets, so that part of their divergence can be read as institutional. But it is not a measure of what Estonia lost. The two economies were already a quarter apart in 1938, and Finland's growth after 1968, \grx{Finland}{1968}{1989} per cent a year, was exceptional by the standards of the Western core (\grx{Western}{1968}{1989} per cent) and of the Nordic countries (\grx{Nordics}{1968}{1989} per cent), driven by a forest-products and engineering complex that Estonia never possessed and by access to a Soviet market on favourable bilateral terms that Estonia, inside the Union, could not exploit.\footnote{; \autocite[23--4]{norkus2016}.} The Western periphery as a whole, the group of poorer Western economies to which Estoni

A FINNISH MIRACLE THAT NEVER WAS % ============================================================= \section{A Finnish miracle that never was} \label{sec:finland} The comparison with Finland has shaped the way Estonians and their historians think about the twentieth century. The two peoples speak related languages, were shaped by Lutheran schooling and Swedish law, emancipated their peasantries early and built co-operative agrarian economies after 1918; in the Soviet period Finland, visible on television from Tallinn, became `proof of what Estonia would have been if the country had not ended up under the Soviet occupation'.\footnote{\autocite[83]{lepppantti2013}.} The scholarly version of the argument has two steps. The first is that the two countries stood at the same level before 1940: Dellenbrant wrote that their levels of development were `close to equal around 1940', Soviet-era comparisons of real wages put Estonian workers ahead of Finnish ones as late as 1966, and the White Book's estimate of the losses of occupation rests on the assumption that Estonia would have followed the Finnish path.\footnote{\autocite[206]{dellenbrant1992}; \autocite[251, 257]{klesment2009}; \autocite[141--74]{kukk2005}.} The second is that the gap observed in 1991, when Estonian living standards were put at 40 per cent of Finland's, measures the cost of Soviet rule.\footnote{\autocite[206]{dellenbrant1992}.} Sceptics have questioned both steps. Kõll argued in 1994 that the belief in Baltic--Nordic parity before the war was `misleading'; an Estonian economist of the 1930s had already written that `Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and even Latvia are ahead of us regarding their wealth'; and Norkus, working from the benchmark estimates, concluded that the gap `cannot only be considered as the legacy of the Soviet occupation'.\footnote{\autocite[201]{koll1994gap}; \autocite[131]{klesment2005}; \autocite[18]{norkus2016}; \autocite[154]{norkus_restorations}.} The new series allows the two steps to be examined year by year. Table~\ref{tab:relative} gives Estonian income per head as a percentage of Finland's at the benchmark years, and Table~\ref{tab:growth} the growth rates between them. In 1913 the two countries were indeed close: Estonia stood at \pctfin{1913} per cent of the Finnish level. In 1919, after wars that had damaged both, Finland the more severely in 1918, it stood at \pctfin{1919} per cent. The parity did not survive the 1920s. Finland grew by \grx{Finland}{1919}{1929} per cent a year to 1929 and Estonia by \gr{1919}{1929} per cent, and by 1929 Estonia was at \pctfin{1929} per cent of the Finnish level; the 1930s, in which Estonia's growth of \gr{1929}{1938} per cent a year was close to Finland's \grx{Finland}{1929}{1938} per cent, left the ratio at \pctfin{1938} per cent in 1938. Clark's 90 per cent, which Valge adopted and which has anchored the literature since, is thus too high by a sixth; Bocharnikova's finding that the purchasing power of wages in Estonia was only 4 per cent below Finland's in 1938 refers to urban wages alone and says nothing about the nearly two-thirds of the Estonian labour force on the land.\footnote{\autocite[81--2]{bocharnikova2021}.} The difference in 1938 was not one of social capability. Table~\ref{tab:structure} shows Estonian literacy above Finnish, Estonian university enrolment per head well above Finnish, and the same share of the labour force in agriculture; Table~\ref{tab:trade} shows both economies open, though Finland more so. The difference is better explained by resources and markets. Finland's forests, sawmills and pulp mills gave it an export staple for which Western demand recovered quickly after 1920 and which carried a growing engineering sector with it; Estonia's butter and bacon faced Danish competition and British quotas, and its industry had lost the only large market it had ever served.\footnote{\autocite[184, 198--200]{finlandeh01}; \autocite[193--210]{koll1994gap}.} The second step of the argument fares no better, though for a different reason. Soviet rule did open a gap, but the timing is not what the argument supposes. Finland lost the Second World War and paid reparations; Estonia was fought over twice and collectivised. In 1950 the ratio stood at \pctfin{1950} per cent, higher than in 1938, and in 1968, after the two decades of Soviet industrialisation examined above, at \pctfin{1968} per cent, the highest level since 1919. Measured against Finland, the first half of Soviet rule was a period of convergence. The divergence that the literature attributes to occupation is a phenomenon of its second half: between 1968 and 1989 Finland grew by \grx{Finland}{1968}{1989} per cent a year, half as fast again as the Western core, and Estonia by \gr{1968}{1989} per cent, so that the ratio fell to \pctfin{1973} per cent in 1973 and \pctfin{1989} per cent in 1989. Those who lived through it dated the divergence correctly: Dellenbrant, drawing on Kukk's calculations, placed its beginning in the late 1960s.\footnote{\autocite[205]{dellenbrant1992}.} What the new series adds is the magnitude. Expressed in logarithms, the Estonian shortfall against Finland was 0.29 in 1938 and 0.63 in 1989; almost half of the gap at the end of Soviet rule had opened before it began, and the whole of the increase after 1938 occurred after 1968. Two conclusions follow. The first concerns the use of Finland as a yardstick. Finland is a revealing comparator for Estonia, because the two economies had similar endowments of human capital, though not of natural resources or markets, so that part of their divergence can be read as institutional. But it is not a measure of what Estonia lost.
